title: Act I, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: On a night of thunder and strange sights (a slave's burning hand that does not burn, a lion near the Capitol, men on fire walking the streets, an owl hooting at noon), Casca meets Cicero and then Cassius. Cassius reads the omens as warnings against Caesar's tyranny and wins Casca to the plot. Cinna joins them; Cassius sends him to place forged letters where Brutus will find them, and they agree that Brutus's good name will make their deed look like virtue.

context.history: Romans read storms and unusual events (prodigies) as messages from the gods. Plutarch records omens before Caesar's death. Cicero, a famous orator, was not part of the plot.

significance: The same omens are read in opposite ways: Casca is terrified, Cassius turns them into an argument. The scene shows that interpretation is itself a tool of persuasion.
discussionQuestions: Do people tend to read signs and news in the way that fits what they already believe?
Where does setting appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with public versus private self?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show storm, omens and recruitment? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of storm, omens and recruitment? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene III develops the idea of storm, omens and recruitment. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of storm, omens and recruitment. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene III suggests about storm, omens and recruitment. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's setting and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses setting in Act I, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of storm, omens and recruitment. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of storm, omens and recruitment responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of storm, omens and recruitment follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene III and its treatment of storm, omens and recruitment. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's setting and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about storm, omens and recruitment in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of storm, omens and recruitment. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

satQuestions.passage:
A common slave—you know him well by sight—
Held up his left hand, which did flame and burn
Like twenty torches join’d, and yet his hand,
Not sensible of fire, remain’d unscorch’d.
Besides—I ha’ not since put up my sword—
Against the Capitol I met a lion,
Who glared upon me, and went surly by,
Without annoying me: and there were drawn
Upon a heap a hundred ghastly women,
Transformed with their fear; who swore they saw
Men all in fire walk up and down the streets.
And yesterday the bird of night did sit
Even at noon-day upon the market-place,
Hooting and shrieking. When these prodigies
Do so conjointly meet, let not men say
“These are their reasons; they are natural;”
For, I believe, they are portentous things
Unto the climate that they point upon.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The storm scene shows that omens can be interpreted however people wish. Useful evidence: “O, he sits high in all the people’s hearts” (Act I, Scene III, Casca (speech 36)): Casca on Brutus's reputation. On characterization: Casca is terrified; Cassius bares his chest to the lightning and interprets the omens as warnings against Caesar. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
